lead: A charter yacht is a small house with an engine, and on a flotilla the lead crew's engineer is a radio call away. Your part is the daily check, reading the alarms correctly and stopping a small fault before it becomes a big one.

sections.title: Two minutes before the first start

blocks.p: Every morning, before the first start, open the engine box and look. It takes two minutes and finds most problems while you are still tied up.

list: Coolant level in the header tank
Drive belt tight and not frayed
Fuel tap on, enough fuel for the day

blocks.p: Yacht engines are **diesels**. Petrol in the tank means draining it, with a fire risk and a damaged engine: at the fuel quay, look at the nozzle yourself. Work out the fuel for a leg before you go: hours under engine times litres an hour, with a reserve left over.

lines: 4 h × 3 L/h = 12 L used, 48 L left

blocks.cap: 20 M ÷ 5 kn = 4 hours. 4 h × 3 L/h = 12 litres, so 48 of the 60 are left.

blocks.p: The engine is cooled by sea water. It comes in through a **seacock**, passes the **raw-water strainer**, is pushed along by a pump with a rubber **impeller** and leaves with the exhaust. So after every start, look over the stern: water must spurt out with the exhaust. No water means no cooling, and you stop the engine.

head: No water: check
What you do
rows: Seacock
Make sure it is open
Strainer
Weed or plastic in the bowl: clean it
Impeller
Intake clear and still no water: the impeller has failed. Stop and call the lead crew

fig.title: Cleaning the strainer
lines: 3. Open the strainer, clean the basket
5. Open the seacock, start, check the exhaust

blocks.rule: Close the seacock before you open the strainer, or the sea pours in. Open it again before you start, or the engine overheats.

sections.title: When the panel shouts, stop the engine

blocks.p: Both alarms ask for the same first action: **stop the engine**. Overheating with steam and little water at the exhaust means the raw-water flow has failed: check the intake. Low oil pressure can wreck a diesel within minutes: stop, check the oil level, and do not restart until you know why.
The one exception is the safety of the boat. Close to a rocky lee shore, unroll the genoa and sail clear first, then stop the engine.
A thump under the stern, heavy vibration and lost speed near fishing floats mean a **rope round the propeller**: go to neutral and stop the engine.

The boat has two battery banks. The **house** bank runs the fridge, lights and instruments; the **engine** battery only starts the engine. At anchor run everything from the house bank and keep the engine battery isolated. With the switch on BOTH the two are joined, and a night of fridge flattens the starting battery as well.

blocks.p: Batteries charge from the engine's **alternator** or from the shore-power charger. A charge light that stays on with the engine running, and a squeal from the engine box, point to a slack or broken alternator belt. On many engines the same belt drives the water pump, so watch the temperature too.
For **shore power**, plug the cable into the boat first and the pillar second, so you never hold a live loose end. To leave, unplug at the pillar first.
Cooking gas is heavier than air. A leak does not blow away: it sinks into the bilge and lies there until a spark finds it. So gas is in the pipe only while you cook.
After cooking, shut the supply first, at the solenoid switch or the bottle valve, and let the flame burn off the gas left in the pipe. Then turn off the burner knob.

fig.title: Smell of gas
lines: Turn the gas off at the bottle
Open every hatch and air the boat

blocks.rule: Supply off, flame dies, then the burner knob.

What it means

The tank is empty
Pump off, switch to the other tank
You are in harbour or at anchor

Pump by hand, then check both

blocks.p: A water pump left running dry can burn out, so switch it off at the panel as soon as the taps spit air.
Find the **manual bilge pump** and its handle on the first day. It works when the electrics do not.
